358: Chapter 3  Underwater Image Super-Resolution Reconstruction Based on a Frequency-Spatial Coupled Inference Network
360: The underwater imaging environment is complex: during propagation, light is simultaneously affected by both absorption and scattering effects, and the degree of attenuation differs markedly for light of different wavelengths. This characteristic causes the underwater images acquired to generally exhibit visual defects such as colour imbalance, low contrast and texture degradation. These degradation phenomena not only affect human intuitive interpretation but also severely constrain the effectiveness of advanced applications such as underwater object detection, path planning and structural inspection. Super-resolution (SR) reconstruction technology, by inferring high-resolution output from low-resolution input, can effectively restore degraded structural and textural components in the image, and is currently an important technical means of improving image quality in underwater vision systems. Thanks to the wide-ranging breakthroughs of deep learning in image restoration, underwater image SR methods based on convolutional neural networks and Transformer architectures have successively emerged [18]. Such methods generally reconstruct high-frequency texture through multi-level spatial feature extraction and cascaded modules, and have achieved good reconstruction results on public datasets. However, the vast majority of the above methods perform feature modelling only within the spatial domain, and their exploitation of the global structural information and periodic patterns contained in the frequency domain remains very limited [32]; when faced with the complex and diverse degradation phenomena of underwater scenes, they struggle to stably capture global contextual cues and high-frequency detail. At the same time, existing methods mostly rely on pixel-level L1 loss or generic perceptual loss in their loss function design [7], and these loss functions have insufficient constraining power over image structural contours and fine textures. According to texture-structure decomposition theory, an image can be represented as the superposition of a structure layer and a texture layer; decoupling the two components and applying supervision to each separately can provide more targeted optimisation guidance during reconstruction [29]. Inspired by this, this chapter introduces a texture-structure joint loss, applying constraints respectively to high-frequency texture detail and low-frequency structural edges, so that the network can likewise recover perceptually realistic and geometrically accurate reconstruction results under complex underwater degradation conditions.
361: Addressing the limitations of existing methods, this chapter proposes a new Frequency-Spatial Coupled Inference Network (FSCIN), which achieves enhanced reconstruction of underwater image super-resolution by fusing frequency and spatial priors. FSCIN integrates the Spatial Frequency Awareness Module (SFAM), which performs joint modelling of the frequency domain and the spatial domain through the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Swin Transformer-based spatial encoding. SFAM aligns amplitude and phase information through dual-branch processing, thereby effectively capturing and enhancing the high-frequency components and global contextual information of the image. In addition, to maintain perceptual fidelity, this chapter also introduces a texture-structure joint constraint loss, which decomposes the reconstructed image into a texture layer and a structure layer and applies targeted supervision to each layer. This loss effectively constrains FSCIN to preserve the integrity of structural boundaries while reconstructing fine-grained visual detail. Extensive experimental results show that FSCIN demonstrates superior performance in reconstructing underwater images with good visual quality and accurate structure.

367: The standard Transformer model faces two prominent bottlenecks when applied to visual tasks: first, the scale of image features varies dynamically with the task, making it difficult to directly apply the fixed-token-size processing paradigm from natural language processing; second, the computational complexity of the global self-attention mechanism is proportional to the square of the image size, making the computational overhead extremely large when processing high-resolution images. Addressing these two limitations, Liu et al. proposed the Swin Transformer, a general-purpose visual backbone network with a hierarchical structure [30], which imitates the multi-scale feature extraction approach of CNNs and restricts self-attention computation within local fixed windows, reducing computational complexity from quadratic to linear while still accounting for the perception of global information. As shown in Figure 3.1 and Figure 3.2, the Swin Transformer is composed of four successively progressive processing stages. The input image is first divided by a Patch Partition operation into a number of two-dimensional image patches of size PxP (P=4), which form a sequence that is fed into the subsequent stages. From the second stage onwards, adjacent patches are merged by the Patch Merging module, which expands the channel dimension while reducing spatial resolution, progressively building a hierarchical feature representation similar to that of a CNN. Each processing stage is composed of several consecutive Swin Transformer blocks, with two adjacent blocks alternately using W-MSA (Window-based MSA) and SW-MSA (Shift-Window-based MSA). W-MSA reduces computation by restricting attention computation within local windows, while SW-MSA introduces a window-shifting mechanism to ensure that information between adjacent windows is effectively transmitted, compensating for the deficiency of purely local window attention in cross-window contextual interaction. Let the input feature map size be H x W and the window size be M x M; the computational complexity of W-MSA can be approximately expressed as O(HW . M2), far lower than the O((HW)2) of global attention, laying the efficiency foundation for practically deploying the Transformer structure in high-resolution visual tasks such as super-resolution.

372: The Fourier transform is a foundational mathematical tool in the field of signal and image processing; its core role is to convert a signal from the spatial domain to the frequency domain, revealing the global periodic structure of the signal in the form of a spectrum. For two-dimensional images, the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is defined as:
373: where f(x, y) is the spatial-domain image, F(u, v) is the corresponding frequency-domain representation, (u, v) are the frequency-domain coordinates, and H, W are respectively the height and width of the image. The frequency-domain representation F(u, v) is in complex form and can be further decomposed into an amplitude spectrum |F(u, v)| and a phase spectrum angle F(u, v): the amplitude spectrum reflects the energy distribution of each frequency component and is closely related to the overall brightness and texture energy of targets in the image; the phase spectrum encodes the spatial position information of each frequency component and plays a key role in the geometric form of image structure.
374: In the super-resolution task, high-frequency components correspond to fine structures in the image such as edges and textures, and are the core determinant of reconstruction quality; low-frequency components correspond to the contours and overall brightness of the image, as shown in Figure 3.3. In engineering practice, the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is generally used, replacing the O(N2) of directly computing the DFT with a time complexity of O(N log N), significantly improving the practical efficiency of frequency-domain transformation within deep networks. After frequency-domain features have been modelled, the Inverse FFT (IFFT) can restore the processed spectrum back to the spatial domain, guaranteeing the spatial consistency of the features. This round-trip transformation mechanism of "spatial domain -> frequency domain -> spatial domain" is the core theoretical basis for the design of the SFAM module in this chapter.

422: The USR-248 dataset was constructed for the underwater single-image super-resolution task. It contains high-resolution images of 640x480 pixels together with their corresponding low-resolution versions at three sizes - 320x240, 160x120 and 80x60 - corresponding respectively to x2, x4 and x8 magnification factors. This dataset contains 1,050 training sample pairs and provides 248 test images for performance evaluation. The image sources cover marine exploration, field acquisition and public online resources; the low-resolution images are generated by simulated degradation, and can reasonably reflect the problem of underwater detail loss under different resolution conditions.
423: The UFO-120 dataset was constructed specifically for underwater image enhancement and super-resolution reconstruction tasks. Its images were collected from multiple marine exploration scenarios, covering different water-body environments and types of visual degradation. This dataset contains 1,500 training sample groups and 120 test sample groups, corresponding to the three upsampling factors x2, x3 and x4. Its low-resolution images are generated through style-transfer perturbation, Gaussian blur and bicubic down-sampling, and can simulate the compound degradation caused by factors such as underwater light attenuation, scattering and imaging-equipment limitations.
425: During training, the Adam optimiser is used to minimise the multi-modal joint loss function, with hyperparameters set to
426: beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, epsilon=10-8, and an initial learning rate of 0.001, decayed at fixed intervals during training. Each mini-batch contains 16 low-resolution image patches of spatial size 50x50 pixels. The model is implemented on the PyTorch framework, and the training platform is an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU.
428: This chapter comprehensively adopts three complementary metrics - Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) and Underwater Image Quality Measure (UIQM) - to quantitatively evaluate super-resolution reconstruction results. PSNR focuses on pixel-level error, SSIM on structural consistency, and UIQM evaluates colour, sharpness and contrast from the perspective of underwater imaging characteristics; combining the three can more comprehensively reflect the objective quality of the reconstructed image and the underwater visual perception effect. Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) measures the pixel-level difference between the reconstructed image and the true high-resolution image based on Mean Squared Error (MSE), and is one of the most commonly used objective evaluation metrics in super-resolution tasks. Its computational formula is:
429: where L denotes the maximum pixel value of the image, usually 255 for an 8-bit image; H and W respectively denote the image height and width; Y is the reconstructed image output by the model, and S is the true high-resolution image. The PSNR value is expressed in dB; the higher the value, the smaller the pixel error between the reconstructed image and the reference image, and the lower the degree of objective distortion [65]. It should be noted that PSNR is relatively sensitive to overall pixel deviation but cannot fully reflect texture naturalness and structural perceptual quality, and therefore must be analysed together with other metrics.
430: Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) measures the degree of similarity between two images along the three dimensions of luminance, contrast and structure. Compared with purely pixel-error metrics, SSIM is closer to the way the human eye perceives changes in image structure. Its computational formula is:
432: where mu_Y and mu_S respectively denote the means of the reconstructed and reference images, sigma_Y
435: variance, and c1 and c2 are stabilising constants introduced to avoid a zero denominator. SSIM values usually lie between 0 and 1; the closer to 1, the more similar the two images are in luminance, contrast and structure [66]. In the underwater image super-resolution task, SSIM reflects well whether edge contours and structural textures have been stably recovered.
436: The Underwater Image Quality Measure (UIQM) is a no-reference image quality evaluation method designed for underwater scenes. It does not rely on a true high-resolution image, but instead comprehensively evaluates image quality from the perspective of underwater visual perception characteristics. UIQM is obtained as a linear weighting of three sub-metrics - colourfulness measure (UICM), sharpness measure (UISM) and contrast measure (UIConM):
438: where UICM measures image colour balance and colour reproduction, UISM evaluates edge and texture sharpness, UIConM reflects local contrast performance, and c1, c2 and c3 are empirical weighting coefficients. The higher the UIQM value, the better the overall performance of the underwater image in terms of colour naturalness, texture sharpness and contrast [67]. Because underwater images are often accompanied by colour casts, low contrast and texture attenuation, UIQM provides an important supplement to PSNR and SSIM for underwater visual quality analysis.
440: To comprehensively evaluate the reconstruction performance of FSCIN, this chapter selects a set of representative methods from the current image super-resolution field as comparison baselines, covering the following categories: traditional CNN methods (SRCNN, VDSR); GAN-based methods (SRGAN [7], SRDRM, SRDRM-GAN); and methods designed specifically for underwater scenes (PAL, AMPCNet [17], DeepWaveNet [19], RDLN). All comparative experiments are conducted under a unified dataset split and identical evaluation metrics, in order to guarantee the fairness of the comparison results.
441: This chapter combines two evaluation approaches, quantitative and qualitative: quantitative analysis makes numerical comparisons based on the three metrics PSNR, SSIM and UIQM; qualitative analysis uses visualised results to intuitively demonstrate the differences between models in edge sharpness, texture fidelity and colour naturalness.

489: Addressing the underwater image super-resolution reconstruction task, this chapter has proposed the Frequency-Spatial Coupled Inference Network (FSCIN) to solve the problems of insufficient exploitation of frequency-domain information and the limited constraining power of loss functions. The network constructs a three-stage processing framework comprising low-level feature extraction, frequency-spatial collaborative feature enhancement and high-resolution image reconstruction; the function of each stage is clear and the coupling is reasonable, providing a good basis for the flexible replacement and extension of subsequent modules. The core spatial-frequency awareness module (SFAM) maps features into the frequency domain through the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), models the amplitude spectrum and phase spectrum separately using a dual-branch Swin Transformer attention structure, and then restores them to the spatial domain through the inverse Fourier transform (IFFT), achieving deep fusion of frequency-domain global perception and spatial-domain local modelling. The joint loss function, which applies supervision separately to the texture layer and the structure layer, effectively improves the reconstruction accuracy of high-frequency detail and geometric edges through the coordinated action of gradient-domain texture constraints and structure-extractor constraints. Experimental results show that FSCIN achieves optimal or highly competitive quantitative metrics at multiple magnification factors on the two public benchmark datasets USR-248 and UFO-120, while also demonstrating clearer texture restoration capability and higher structural fidelity in visual quality, providing a high-quality image pre-processing basis for the subsequent underwater object detection task.
